clinical_category: Oncology supportive care - radiation skin injury
stem: During external-beam radiation therapy, a client develops an area in the treatment field where the skin is peeling, moist, and painful. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Notify the radiation oncology team, assess the skin for severity and infection concerns, and follow the team's gentle cleansing and prescribed dressing plan for the moist reaction.
options.B: Scrub the moist area vigorously during bathing to remove loose skin and reduce bacterial growth.
options.C: Apply an adhesive bandage and any over-the-counter antibiotic ointment available without first checking the radiation skin-care plan.
options.D: Reassure the client that wet, painful skin breakdown does not need to be reported because it is an expected finding that cannot be treated.

rationale: A is correct. NCI defines a moist reaction as radiation-related skin peeling that becomes moist and painful; sores or ulcers may develop and can lead to infection. NCI advises clients to report skin changes promptly and states that the health care team may direct how to keep a peeling, painful, wet area clean and dry and may prescribe special dressings or antibiotics when indicated. B is incorrect because vigorous scrubbing can further injure damaged skin. C is incorrect because unapproved adhesives and self-selected topical products should not be placed over irradiated skin without the radiation team's plan. D is incorrect because a moist reaction requires assessment and directed supportive care rather than dismissal.
educational_objective: Recognize a moist radiation skin reaction and provide prompt assessment plus radiation-team-directed gentle skin/wound care rather than vigorous cleansing or unsupervised adhesive/topical treatment.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Skin and Nail Changes during Cancer Treatment; NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — moist reaction; External Beam Radiation Therapy for Cancer
source_locator: NCI Dictionary entry 'moist reaction'; Skin and Nail Changes — opening radiation-therapy skin-change paragraph plus 'Ways to prevent or manage mild skin and nail changes' bullets 'Prevent infection' and 'Protect your skin'; External Beam Radiation Therapy — skin-care instructions near the treatment area, including avoidance of tight clothing and adhesive bandages.
source_claim_supported: Moist reaction is peeling, moist, painful irradiated skin with possible sores/infection; skin changes should be reported; the team directs cleaning and prescribed dressings/treatment; adhesives and trauma to the field should be avoided.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — skin care, hygiene and comfort interventions for treatment-related skin breakdown; integrated nursing process includes assessment and implementation of appropriate supportive care.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's general preventive skin-care item into recognition and management of an actual moist radiation reaction, avoiding duplication and removing vague blanket instructions in favor of NCI-supported assessment and team-directed care.
audit_findings: NCI directly defines the stem findings as a moist reaction and identifies possible ulceration/infection.
NCI directs prompt reporting and team-guided cleaning/dressings rather than self-treatment or vigorous scrubbing.
The key is deliberately action-based and avoids prescribing a universal dressing product unsupported by the source.
Distractors reflect realistic radiation-skin-care errors and no alternative is defensible.
Independent adversarial review found no second answer, cueing, unsupported dressing mandate, locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or unresolved conflict.
